title: Hearing Louis Armstrong's records and arranging his tunes
summary: He had no night off to hear the river-boat bands, but knew Armstrong's Hot Five records and Snag It, made arrangements of Armstrong tunes, and was moved by the Bessie Smith St. Louis Blues record.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: When you were in St. Louis, did you hear any of the New Orleans bands on the boats?
Unfortunately I didn't get a chance to get to the boats. No. Because playing at the theater I was playing every night, didn't have a night off. Then when I was at the Club I didn't have a night off.
Had you heard any of the records -- by this time the Oliver Creole Jazz Band records were out. You had mentioned Snag -- How did you learn Snag?

Yes, I heard Louie -- I had heard Louie and Oliver -- I had heard Louie's record and after hearing Louie, oh, I made arrangements of a lot of Louie's stuff. I made arrangements on Snag for the band that we played with. I made arrangements on that.
Yeah, but that was Oliver's tune. What did you hear of Louie -- did you hear the Louie Hot Fives by this time?

Yes. I heard Louie Hot Five, I heard "Cornet Chop Suey," and I used to play the "Cornet Chop Suey" and the "Oriental Strut" -- I used to play that, that "Oriental Strut" was pretty too. And the Strut was (unintelligible). Yes, all those Louie tunes.
Were you patterning your playing on Louie at this time?
I think I just leaned toward Louie then
after hearing Louie -- I'll tell you what I heard. I heard Louie and Bessie Smith once. Someone played the organ --
yes, the St. Louis Blues -- Fred Longshaw.
-- played a little organ and Louie was playing the trumpet and Bessie Smith was singing, and I never heard such thing --
A very moving record. The St. Louis Blues, the three of them doing that.
And Louie was playing -- Louie was really playing some pretty horn.
